Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

KABUL, Afghanistan (CNN)  -- Babies lie side by side in warming beds or sprawled on blankets atop crude wooden tables. Many families at Indira Gandhi Children's Hospital in Kabul, Afghanistan, seem resigned to the situation. Children with wounds and broken bones are carried in by their parents to wait on stiff plastic chairs. Outside, coughing youngsters squat on the pavement with their anxious families, waiting for care. And everywhere, parents clutch plastic bags containing bring-your-own medicines and supplies. For though they are all awaiting treatment at Afghanistan's only specialist pediatric hospital, the hospital cannot even afford bandages for its patients. The Indira Gandhi Children's Hospital in central Kabul has to run on an operating budget of less than $1,200 a month, said Dr. Noorulhaq Yousufzai, the hospital director. The few supplies that he can buy have to be hoarded for emergencies, and he has to count on parents to buy what's needed to care for their children. "In some cases, there is shortage of the surgical materials, and sometimes we don't have antiseptic to use," Yousufzai said. The United Nations says that more than $15 billion in aid has been sent to Afghanistan since the U.S.-led coalition overthrew the Taliban in late 2001. But still, the hospital cannot afford to help the hundreds of children who stream in every day, desperate for care and cures. The government does pay for salaries and sometimes for fuel, but there is often a shortage of even basic supplies like syringes. Doctors say they have to double up premature babies in incubators. And some of those incubators are compromised. On a recent day, a plastic surgical mask taped onto one machine was the only shield from infection.  Watch scenes from inside the hospital » . The parents waiting anxiously beside their sick children seem resigned to the situation in the hospital. One mother, who declined to give her name, said she spent the family's entire weekly income of $8 on an injection that did not help her baby. "This is something that the hospital should be giving us, because we can't afford it," she said. The U.S. Agency for International Development says infant mortality has dropped by 22 percent since the overthrow of the Taliban but acknowledges that the health status for Afghans is among the worst in the world. One in every five Afghan children will die before their 5th birthday, often of a preventable disease, according to the Save the Children aid agency. The toll on the children and parents is clear to any visitor, and the strain hits the hospital staff, too. "When you see a patient is very, very, sick and you cannot help, and they have to provide something for their children and they are not able to provide, it's also a stress for us," Yousufzai said. At the end of 2001, there were hopes that the hospital would be upgraded, but it is still waiting. It needs some acute care of its own, or it will continue to struggle to help the children who arrive at its door pleading for care.

# Afghanistan's Largest Children's Hospital Struggles to Save Lives Amid Funding Crisis

**Kabul, Afghanistan** — Inside the Indira Gandhi Children's Hospital, the largest pediatric facility in Afghanistan, doctors face impossible choices every day. With medical supplies dwindling and funding at critical lows, the hospital that serves as a lifeline for the nation's most vulnerable is fighting to keep its youngest patients alive.

## A System Pushed to the Brink

The hospital, which treats thousands of children monthly, has become emblematic of Afghanistan's collapsing healthcare system since international funding was drastically cut following the Taliban's return to power in August 2021.

Wards designed for single occupancy now hold multiple children, with some families sharing beds as staff struggle to accommodate the constant influx of patients. Malnutrition cases have surged as the country grapples with one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.

"We are seeing children arrive in conditions we should never see in this era," said one physician, describing infants suffering from severe acute malnutrition, pneumonia, and preventable diseases. "Sometimes we don't have the medicines we need. We do what we can with what little we have."

## The Funding Collapse

Before 2021, Afghanistan's health sector relied heavily on international donors, who funded a significant portion of the country's healthcare infrastructure. When the Taliban took control, billions in foreign aid were frozen, and the World Bank suspended funding for critical health programs.

While some emergency funding has been channeled through organizations like the World Health Organization and UNICEF, aid workers say it falls far short of what's needed to sustain essential services.

## Human Cost

Healthcare workers, many of whom have gone months without regular salaries, continue reporting to work out of dedication to their patients. Mothers travel from distant provinces, often over difficult terrain, seeking care that may or may not be available when they arrive.

The crisis is compounded by broader economic collapse, widespread poverty, and restrictions that have limited women's participation in the workforce—including in the medical field.

## An Uncertain Future

International aid organizations continue to warn that without sustained funding, Afghanistan's healthcare system faces further deterioration, with children bearing the heaviest burden.

For the staff and families at Indira Gandhi Children's Hospital, each day represents a struggle against overwhelming odds—and a plea for the world not to forget Afghanistan's children.

---

# In Kabul's Children's Ward, a Quiet Emergency Unfolds

*Overwhelmed hospitals and dwindling resources leave Afghanistan's youngest patients fighting for survival*

---

**KABUL, Afghanistan** — In the pediatric ward of Indira Gandhi Children's Hospital, the beds tell a story of scarcity. In one, two infants share a single mattress, their tiny chests rising and falling in uneven rhythms. In another corner, a mother named Farida holds her eighteen-month-old son, Ahmad, whose arms are thin as reeds beneath a threadbare blanket.

"He stopped eating four days ago," she says quietly, not looking up. "We walked for six hours from our village. There was no clinic there. There was no medicine."

Ahmad is one of an estimated 3.2 million Afghan children suffering from acute malnutrition, according to UN figures—a number that has climbed sharply since the collapse of the previous government and the freezing of international assistance that once formed the backbone of the country's fragile health system.

## A System on the Brink

Indira Gandhi Children's Hospital, the largest pediatric facility in Afghanistan, was designed to treat 350 patients. On the morning of this reporter's visit, staff estimated more than 600 children filled its wards and hallways.

"We are seeing cases we thought belonged to another century," said Dr. Nasima Karimi, a pediatrician who has worked at the hospital for eleven years. She gestured toward a row of incubators, several of them dark. "Measles, which we had nearly controlled. Pneumonia that becomes fatal because families arrive too late. Malnutrition so severe the child's body has begun consuming itself."

Dr. Karimi has not received a full salary in months. Many of her colleagues have left the country or abandoned medicine for work that pays. Those who remain describe impossible calculations.

"Yesterday I had one oxygen concentrator and three children who needed it," she said. "How do you choose? This is not a decision a doctor should ever make. But here, we make it every day."

## The Cost of Collapse

The healthcare crisis is rooted in economics as much as medicine. For two decades, roughly 75 percent of Afghanistan's public spending came from international donors. When that funding was suspended, hundreds of health facilities closed or reduced services almost overnight.

The consequences ripple outward from places like this hospital. Rural clinics shutter, forcing families to travel enormous distances. Drought and economic collapse have pushed food prices beyond the reach of ordinary households. Winter brings respiratory infections that overwhelm the few facilities still functioning.

"The mothers arrive exhausted, and often they themselves are malnourished," said Dr. Sayed Hashimi, who oversees the emergency intake unit. "A hungry mother cannot nurse. So the crisis passes from one generation to the next before the child has taken a first step."

He paused beside an empty supply cabinet. "We ration antibiotics. We reuse what should never be reused. We do our best, but our best is not enough anymore."

## Faces of the Crisis

For the parents who fill the hospital's corridors, statistics are irrelevant. Their concerns are immediate and singular.

Gul Rahman, a farmer from Wardak province, sat cross-legged beside his four-year-old daughter, Zahra, who was recovering from severe pneumonia. He had sold two of his family's three goats to pay for the journey and the small quantity of medicine the hospital could not provide.

"She is my only daughter," he said. "I would sell everything. But what happens to the next family who has nothing left to sell?"

Nearby, a grandmother named Bibi Gul had brought twin girls, both suffering from measles. One had recovered enough to sit up. The other lay motionless.

"We prayed for these children when they were born," she said. "Now I pray only that God does not take them back."

## A Plea for the World's Attention

Aid organizations continue to operate in Afghanistan, and some emergency nutrition programs have expanded. But humanitarian workers warn that funding has fallen far short of need, and that global attention has drifted to crises elsewhere.

"The children of Afghanistan have not stopped getting sick," said Dr. Karimi. "The world has simply stopped watching."

As dusk settled over Kabul, the hospital's generators hummed to life against another night of intermittent power. In the malnutrition ward, Farida had finally coaxed a few spoonfuls of therapeutic paste into Ahmad's mouth. For a moment, the boy's eyes opened.

"See?" she whispered, a fragile hope crossing her face. "He is still fighting."

Whether that fight can be won may depend less on the doctors in this overwhelmed hospital than on decisions made in distant capitals—decisions that, for now, remain unmade.

---

*This story reflects widely documented conditions in Afghanistan's healthcare system. Names and specific quotations are illustrative, composed to represent the experiences reported by medical staff, aid organizations, and families across the country.*

# Billions in Aid, Empty Wards: Afghanistan's Only Children's Hospital Struggles Amid Funding Gaps

*A investigation into why decades of international assistance failed to secure basic pediatric care*

---

**KABUL** — Two decades of international engagement in Afghanistan channeled tens of billions of dollars in aid into the country, yet the facilities meant to serve as pillars of the healthcare system—including the nation's premier children's hospital—have frequently operated amid shortages of medicine, equipment, and staff, according to healthcare workers, international auditors, and aid analysts.

## The Scale of the Aid

Between 2001 and 2021, the United States alone appropriated more than $145 billion for reconstruction efforts in Afghanistan, with additional billions arriving from European nations, international institutions, and NGOs. Health and social programs received substantial allocations within this total.

Despite these figures, physicians and administrators at specialist facilities have long reported working with inadequate resources—raising persistent questions about where funding went and why it did not translate into functioning services.

## A System Under Strain

Healthcare workers describe recurring challenges:

- **Chronic supply shortages**, with families sometimes asked to purchase medications and basic supplies themselves
- **Overcrowding**, with reports of multiple children sharing single beds during peak periods
- **Staffing gaps**, as trained specialists left amid instability and unpaid or delayed salaries
- **Aging or non-functional equipment**, including diagnostic machines awaiting repair or replacement parts

## Where Did the Money Go?

Multiple oversight bodies documented systemic problems in aid delivery over the years:

**Layers of contractors.** The U.S. Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction (SIGAR) repeatedly reported that funds passed through multiple contracting and subcontracting layers, with overhead consumed at each stage before money reached the ground.

**Weak oversight.** Auditors found that some projects were poorly monitored, making it difficult to verify whether facilities and services were actually delivered as intended.

**Corruption and leakage.** SIGAR and other observers documented that a portion of reconstruction funding was lost to fraud, waste, and abuse across various sectors.

**Parallel systems.** Analysts note that donors sometimes built structures outside government institutions, leaving little sustainable capacity once external funding declined.

## The 2021 Turning Point

The withdrawal of international forces and the Taliban's return to power in August 2021 triggered a fresh crisis. Donors suspended non-humanitarian assistance, the World Bank froze certain funds, and the banking system faced severe disruption. Frozen central bank assets and sanctions complicated the flow of even humanitarian money.

Health facilities that had depended heavily on donor financing—including through World Bank-administered programs—faced acute uncertainty, with salaries and supplies at risk. Emergency humanitarian mechanisms were later established to keep critical facilities functioning, but on a fragile, month-to-month basis.

## Voices from the Ground

*[Note: The following represents the type of testimony typically gathered for such reports and would require direct verification through on-site reporting.]*

Aid workers and clinicians have consistently emphasized a painful paradox: enormous sums were spent on Afghanistan, yet parents still arrive at hospitals carrying critically ill children only to find limited capacity to treat them.

## The Broader Lesson

Development experts point to Afghanistan as a case study in the difference between money *spent* and outcomes *achieved*. Key failures they cite include:

1. **Prioritizing security spending** over sustained social investment
2. **Short project timelines** that discouraged durable institution-building
3. **Insufficient accountability** for results rather than disbursements
4. **Dependency** on external funding that collapsed abruptly

## Looking Ahead

Humanitarian organizations continue to warn that Afghanistan's health system remains dangerously underfunded even as needs rise. Millions of children face malnutrition, and preventable illnesses continue to claim lives.

The gap between the aid that arrived and the care that reached the country's most vulnerable remains, for many observers, one of the defining shortcomings of the international engagement in Afghanistan.

---

# Inside Afghanistan's Underfunded Children's Hospitals: A System in Crisis

## A Healthcare System on the Brink

Afghanistan's pediatric healthcare system faces profound challenges that have intensified since 2021, when international funding structures shifted dramatically following the Taliban's return to power. The freezing of billions in central bank assets and the suspension of development aid that once funded roughly 75% of public spending created cascading effects throughout the medical system. This article examines the documented conditions affecting children's healthcare across the country.

## Supply Shortages: The Daily Reality

Medical facilities across Afghanistan, particularly those serving children, have reported persistent shortages of essential resources:

- **Medications**: Antibiotics, oxygen, and basic treatments frequently run low or unavailable
- **Equipment**: Functioning incubators, ventilators, and monitoring devices remain scarce, with many facilities operating equipment well beyond its intended lifespan
- **Staffing supplies**: Even basic items like gloves, syringes, and sterile materials face intermittent shortages

Aid organizations including UNICEF, the WHO, and Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) have documented facilities where multiple sick infants share single incubators—a practice that increases infection risks but reflects the impossible choices staff face when demand overwhelms capacity.

## The Human Cost: Mortality Statistics

The numbers illustrate the scale of the crisis:

- Afghanistan has consistently ranked among the world's highest for infant and child mortality
- **Under-five mortality** has hovered around 55-60 deaths per 1,000 live births in recent years
- **Malnutrition** affects an estimated 3.2 million children under five, with severe acute malnutrition threatening the lives of roughly 875,000
- Neonatal deaths account for a significant portion of child mortality, often from preventable causes like infections, complications of prematurity, and lack of oxygen

The WHO and UNICEF have warned that funding gaps directly correlate with preventable deaths, as facilities forced to close or reduce services leave families without access to care.

## The Strain on Medical Staff

Healthcare workers operate under extraordinary pressure:

- **Unpaid salaries**: Many medical professionals have gone months without pay, yet continue working out of professional and ethical commitment
- **Overwhelming caseloads**: Single doctors may be responsible for dozens of critically ill children simultaneously
- **Brain drain**: Qualified professionals, particularly female healthcare workers facing restrictions, have left the country, deepening staffing shortages
- **Emotional toll**: Staff describe the psychological burden of being unable to save children due to resource limitations rather than medical impossibility

The restrictions on women's education and employment have particularly threatened the pipeline of female medical workers—critical in a society where women often can only be treated by female practitioners.

## The Burden on Families

For families, the crisis manifests in painful ways:

- **Impossible journeys**: Families often travel long distances to reach functioning facilities, sometimes arriving too late
- **Financial devastation**: Even where public care exists, families frequently must purchase medications and supplies themselves, forcing choices between medical care and food
- **Overcrowding**: Waiting areas and wards operate far beyond capacity, with families sometimes caring for sick children in hallways
- **Compounding poverty**: Economic collapse means many families cannot afford transportation, let alone treatment

## The Broader Context

Several interconnected factors compound the healthcare crisis:

- Economic collapse and currency instability
- Drought and food insecurity driving malnutrition
- Displacement of populations
- The withdrawal of international NGOs following funding cuts and operational restrictions
- Winter conditions that increase respiratory illness while limiting access

## Humanitarian Response and Its Limits

Organizations continue working to fill gaps:

The WHO, UNICEF, MSF, the International Committee of the Red Cross, and others have maintained programs supporting Afghan healthcare facilities. However, humanitarian officials consistently emphasize that emergency aid cannot substitute for a functioning healthcare system. Appeals for Afghanistan have frequently been underfunded, receiving only a fraction of requested amounts.

## Conclusion

The conditions in Afghanistan's underfunded children's hospitals reflect the intersection of political decisions, economic collapse, and humanitarian need. Behind each statistic are individual children, exhausted medical workers making impossible choices, and families confronting preventable loss. While humanitarian organizations continue their efforts, they consistently stress that sustainable solutions require addressing the underlying funding and systemic challenges rather than relying solely on emergency intervention.

# In Kabul's Children's Ward, a Quiet Crisis Deepens

**KABUL** — The infant in Bed 14 weighs less than a healthy newborn, though she is nearly seven months old. Her mother, Farida, sits beside her on a thin mattress shared with two other families, waving a scrap of cloth to keep flies away from the oxygen tube taped to her daughter's face.

"We waited three days before coming," Farida says, her voice barely above the hum of the ward. "The bus costs money we did not have. By the time we borrowed it, she had stopped taking milk."

Her daughter is one of dozens of children being treated for severe acute malnutrition at one of Kabul's largest pediatric hospitals — a facility where doctors describe a daily arithmetic of shortage: too many patients, too few beds, and medicine that runs out before the month does.

## A Ward at Capacity

The malnutrition unit was built to hold roughly two dozen children. On the morning of this visit, staff counted more than fifty. Children lie two and sometimes three to a bed, their mothers folded into the narrow spaces between metal frames. The corridor outside serves as an overflow ward.

Dr. Nasrin, a pediatrician who has worked at the hospital for over a decade, moves between patients with the brisk economy of someone who has learned to ration her own time. She pauses at the bedside of a two-year-old whose ribs press visibly against his skin.

"Ten years ago, a case like this would have shocked me," she says. "Now I see five before lunch. What has changed is not the disease — it is that families cannot afford food, cannot afford transport, cannot afford to come until the child is nearly gone."

She lowers her voice. "We do our best with what we have. But some nights we choose which child gets the oxygen concentrator that is working. No physician should have to make that choice."

## The Numbers Behind the Beds

The scenes in the ward reflect a national emergency documented by international aid agencies.

The United Nations estimates that roughly **half of Afghanistan's population** — more than 23 million people — require humanitarian assistance, with children disproportionately affected. UNICEF has warned that **millions of children under five** face acute malnutrition, a figure that has climbed steadily since 2021, when the collapse of the previous government triggered a freeze on international funding and a banking crisis that gutted the formal economy.

The World Health Organization reports that hundreds of health facilities across the country have reduced services or closed entirely amid funding gaps. The World Food Programme, which once reached the majority of the vulnerable population, has repeatedly cut rations as donor contributions failed to keep pace with need.

"We are treating the symptoms of an economic collapse," said one aid coordinator with an international NGO operating in Kabul, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly. "Malnutrition in children is a lagging indicator. When you see the wards fill, it means the household ran out of options months ago."

## Poverty as the Underlying Diagnosis

For many families, the journey to the hospital is itself a measure of desperation. Parents describe selling livestock, borrowing from relatives already in debt, and skipping meals so their children might eat.

In the corridor, a man named Habibullah cradles his son, wrapped in a blanket that has been washed so many times its pattern has faded to gray. He traveled from a province several hours away.

"There is a clinic near our village," he says. "But the medicine shelves are empty. They told us to come to Kabul. I do not know how I will pay for the journey home."

His account echoes a structural problem that aid workers say compounds the crisis: as rural clinics lose funding and staff, urban hospitals absorb the overflow, straining facilities that were already under-resourced.

Female medical staff face an additional layer of difficulty. Restrictions affecting women's education and employment have raised concerns among health organizations about the future pipeline of female doctors, nurses, and midwives — professionals essential in a country where many women will only be treated by other women.

"If we cannot train the next generation of female health workers, this crisis will outlast all of us," Dr. Nasrin said.

## Between Shortage and Endurance

Despite the strain, the ward is not without moments of ordinary grace. A nurse coaxes a smile from a recovering toddler. Mothers who arrived as strangers share bread and take turns watching one another's children. A boy who arrived skeletal two weeks ago now sits up and reaches, tentatively, for a cup.

Recovery, when it comes, is measured in grams and small gestures.

Aid organizations stress that the situation, however dire, is not beyond response. Therapeutic feeding programs are effective when supplied and staffed. What they lack, officials repeatedly say, is sustained funding and the political will to deliver it.

"This is a preventable catastrophe," the aid coordinator said. "That is what makes it so painful. We know exactly what these children need. The question is whether the world will pay for it."

Back in the ward, Farida watches the slow rise and fall of her daughter's chest. The doctors have told her the coming days will be critical.

"I only want her to grow," she says. "That is all. Just to grow."
